messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Call Center Agent
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Stress: Stress, Idealized Families: Happy families
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Malia is a 22-year-old married woman of South Eastern Asian descent who works as a call center agent. She came to therapy at the urging of her husband, after months of what she described as "falling apart" in ways she could no longer hide. The traumatic event that shattered her sense of safety occurred eighteen months earlier, when she was still living with her parents and commuting to a previous job at a small retail store. One evening after her shift ended, she was walking to her car in the dimly lit parking lot when a man she did not recognize approached her from behind. He pressed something sharp against her back, forced her into the backseat of her own car, and sexually assaulted her. She remembers fragments of the assault—the feeling of the car upholstery against her cheek, the sound of her own breathing, the taste of bile rising in her throat—but the pieces do not fit together into a coherent sequence. What she remembers most vividly is the taste of blood and dirt that flooded her mouth when he covered her face with his hand, and that taste still returns to her without warning, as real and immediate as if it were happening again, more vivid than any ordinary memory.

In the weeks afterward, Malia tried to push the event out of her mind entirely. She told herself that if she thought about it, she would not be able to handle it—that the memory would break something inside her permanently. She stopped walking to her car alone, then stopped driving altogether, eventually quitting her job. She moved in with her husband, whom she had been dating at the time, and got married sooner than they had planned. She found work at a call center, where she sits in a cubicle with her back to the wall and her eyes fixed on the exit sign. Every room she enters, she scans for the nearest door. Every unexpected movement near her desk makes her flinch as if she is about to be grabbed. She has come to believe that she must be on guard at all times, because danger could come from anywhere, and that she is fundamentally inadequate—that she failed to protect herself, that she missed some sign she should have seen.

The triggers that ambush her are not always obvious. Ambulances are the worst: the first time she heard a siren after the assault, she was in a grocery store and dropped a jar of pasta sauce, shattering it on the floor. Now she wears noise-canceling headphones whenever she leaves the house, even for short errands. Stress of any kind—a difficult call at work, an argument with her husband, even a traffic jam—tends to tip her into a state where the fragmented pieces of the memory start surfacing, and she has to fight to keep them down. But the most confusing trigger is happy families. When she sees a mother pushing a stroller, or a father laughing with his children at a park, she feels a surge of something that is part grief, part rage, part shame. Before the assault, she had imagined having children of her own someday. Now the sight of an intact, happy family makes her feel like she has been permanently excluded from that world.

To cope, Malia has developed strategies that make sense to her but are beginning to worry her husband. She avoids any conversation that might turn toward the event; if a friend or coworker brings up something related to trauma or crime, she changes the subject or walks away. She has become deeply uncomfortable around authority figures—police officers, security guards, even her own building's superintendent—because the uniform triggers a sense of threat she cannot override. And she has started using sexual activity and sexual fantasies as a way to release the tension that builds up inside her throughout the day. At first, this felt like reclaiming something; now she notices that she often dissociates during sex, and her husband has begun to ask if she is actually present with him.

At work, she has started taking her breaks in a locked bathroom stall because the open break room feels too exposed. Her supervisor has commented on her frequent sick days and her tendency to startle during calls. Malia knows she is barely holding things together. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment last week when she saw an ambulance on her commute and pulled over to the side of the road, shaking so badly she could not drive for twenty minutes. She sat in her car, tasting blood and dirt, and thought: I cannot keep living like this. She is terrified that talking about the event will make it worse, that she will lose control entirely, but she is also desperate to stop scanning, stop flinching, stop feeling like a stranger in her own life.
